opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's useful to separate the two. MMLU was designed back in 2020, and at the time models were scoring around chance, roughly 25 percent. The idea was to cover a wide range of subjects, from law and medicine to mathematics and history, at roughly the level of an undergraduate or early professional exam. That benchmark is now essentially saturated. Frontier models score at or above the level of human domain experts across most of those subjects, and the remaining errors are often due to label noise or ambiguous questions rather than genuine gaps in knowledge. So in the sense of broad, exam-style academic knowledge, I think it's fair to say models have exceeded the typical human, and arguably most experts, since almost no person is an expert in all 57 subjects at once.

Humanity's Last Exam was our attempt to build something much harder, because benchmarks were saturating so quickly that we were losing the ability to measure progress at the frontier. We gathered questions from experts around the world, and the bar was that the questions had to stump the best models at the time. These are questions at the edge of human knowledge: research-level mathematics, obscure areas of the sciences and humanities. When we released it, models scored in the single digits, and scores have been climbing quite rapidly since then. I wouldn't be surprised if they eventually reach very high accuracy on it.

But I'd caution people against reading too much into that. Doing well on Humanity's Last Exam means a model can answer closed-ended, verifiable, expert-level questions. It doesn't mean the model can do autonomous research, run a lab, or carry out long-horizon tasks in the real world. Those are different capabilities. So I'd say we're seeing AI exceed humans on knowledge and on certain kinds of reasoning, while still lagging in areas like long-horizon agency, reliability, robustly learning from experience, and some aspects of visual and spatial understanding. The capability profile is very jagged.

That's partly why I think we need to move toward evaluations that measure economically relevant and autonomous capabilities more directly, such as whether a system can complete real tasks that people get paid to do, end to end. Those are much better indicators of the societal impact, and of the risks, than another multiple-choice exam. Exams were a great proxy for a while, but we're approaching the point where they stop telling us what we most need to know.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes MMLU as spanning 57 subjects and says almost no person is an expert in all of them at once, explaining why models can outperform individual humans on the benchmark.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the short version is that on MMLU, that's already happened. We released it back in 2020, and at the time GPT-3 was scoring in the 40s, barely above chance on a lot of the subjects. The idea was to test broad knowledge across fifty-something fields, everything from college chemistry to law to philosophy. Within a few years the frontier models were in the high 80s, low 90s, which is roughly where you'd expect a very strong domain expert to land, and the remaining gap is mostly label noise and a few ambiguous questions. So MMLU is saturated. It stopped being informative about the frontier a while ago, which is exactly why we built Humanity's Last Exam.

The motivation for HLE was that we needed something at the ceiling of human expertise rather than at the level of a well-read undergraduate. So we crowdsourced questions from thousands of researchers, professors, and PhDs around the world, and we specifically filtered for questions that the frontier models at the time got wrong. These are things like niche problems in mathematics, obscure classics translation, specialized chemistry, the kind of question where you basically need to be one of a few hundred people in the world to answer it off the top of your head. When it launched, the best models were in the single digits.

That didn't last. Scores climbed into the 20s and then higher fairly quickly, especially once models got reasoning and tool use. And I'd expect that trend to continue. The way I'd frame it is that there's a difference between exceeding any individual human and exceeding humanity. No single person could score well on HLE, because nobody is simultaneously an expert in Byzantine history and algebraic topology and organic synthesis. So in a sense the models are already superhuman in breadth. What they haven't done is exceed the best human in each domain on their home turf, and that's what the ceiling on HLE represents. Once models are getting most of those questions right, the benchmark is telling you they've matched the aggregate of human expert knowledge.

But I'd add a caveat, which is that these are tests of knowledge and closed-form reasoning. They're measuring whether you know the answer to a well-posed question. They are not measuring whether you can run a research program for six months, or notice that the question was the wrong one to ask, or do the kind of long-horizon, messy, agentic work that actually makes up most of what experts do. So I think we'll see models blow past human performance on exam-style benchmarks, including HLE, before we see them do the full job of an expert. And people shouldn't confuse the first thing for the second. The exam is the last exam in the sense that it's the last academic-style test we can usefully build, not in the sense that passing it means the work is done.

r001.rationale: The response describes MMLU as covering many fields, but says no individual could score well on HLE because of its breadth. It does not connect MMLU’s subject diversity to an individual human being unable to match AI performance on MMLU.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish exceeding human performance on a benchmark from exceeding human capabilities broadly. MMLU tests a fairly wide range of academic knowledge, but once models get very high scores, it becomes less useful for distinguishing their capabilities. That motivates harder evaluations like Humanity’s Last Exam, which pushes toward questions that require much more specialized expertise.

The comparison also depends on which humans you mean. An individual person has a relatively narrow area of expertise. A model can potentially answer questions across many fields, so its breadth can exceed that of any one person even while it remains weaker than the best specialists in particular areas.

I’d expect progress on these harder benchmarks to continue, but I wouldn’t equate a high score with being able to do everything a researcher does. Answering a well-posed question is different from identifying an important problem, developing a useful new approach, and carrying a project through reliably. Those are capabilities we need to evaluate separately.

r001.rationale: The response says MMLU covers a wide range of academic knowledge, then explains that an individual has narrow expertise while a model can answer across many fields and exceed any one person in breadth.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should distinguish between exceeding human performance on a benchmark and exceeding human capabilities broadly. MMLU samples knowledge across a lot of subjects, but once models get very high scores, it becomes less useful for telling us where the frontier is. That’s part of the motivation for Humanity’s Last Exam: asking much harder questions that require specialized expertise, so we have more room to measure progress.

But even if a model does extremely well on that, it doesn’t mean it can do everything a researcher can do. Answering a well-defined question is different from choosing a fruitful research direction, developing a new theory, or carrying out a long project reliably. I’d expect progress to be uneven: systems can become superhuman at some kinds of questions while still making surprisingly basic mistakes elsewhere.

So I’d look at these benchmarks as useful measurements, alongside evidence about what systems can actually accomplish in the world. A high score is significant, but it isn’t a complete account of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says MMLU covers many subjects, but does not suggest that this breadth explains why no individual human could match AI performance.
